investigacion.base:
I couldn't find a live NHC advisory showing a hurricane expected in the October 15–17 window. As of October 7 the question would resolve **No**. Hurricane Rachel is active now but is unlikely to last until October 15, so the outcome depends on whether a new system forms and strengthens in the next week. That hinges on the still-unformed Sergio.

**What the resolution sources say**
- **NHC (?epac):** The NHC Central Pacific outlook issued 8 AM HST on Tuesday, October 6 said NHC was issuing advisories on Hurricane Rachel, located several hundred miles west-southwest of the southern tip of the Baja California Peninsula (translated from Spanish). For the Central Pacific (140°W–180°), no tropical cyclone formation is expected over the next 7 days. I couldn't get the Eastern Pacific outlook text itself, so I can't confirm the current NHC odds for Sergio. Check it directly.
- **NHC season summary (as of October 4):** 17 named storms (+4 vs normal), 7 hurricanes (0), 5 majors (+2), ACE 184.1 (+93%).
- **Metaculus FAQ:** I didn't retrieve it. It only defines "credible sources" as a backup if NHC's site is down, so it doesn't affect the outcome.

**Recent news**
- **October 4 (Ryan Maue):** Hurricane Rachel was at 90 knots (Category 2), heading west. As Rachel moves away from Mexico, another system is forming south of Mexico and will be named Sergio. Sergio's circulation may also help spin up a possible storm in the Gulf of Mexico (NHC gave that 40%).
- **Rachel:** Still a hurricane on October 6, but it's moving west toward cooler water and the 140°W line. Unless it lasts unusually long, it should weaken or leave the basin well before October 15. The key is Sergio's timing: if it forms around October 7–10 and becomes a hurricane, it could still be one on October 15–17.
- **Season backdrop (October 5):** Across the central and eastern Pacific there have been 20 named storms, including 10 hurricanes. The very strong El Niño has helped produce three Category 5 hurricanes. El Niño tends to extend Eastern Pacific activity into October.
- Watch out: a "2026 Pacific hurricane season" fan wiki (hypotheticalhurricanes.fandom) describes made-up storms, including a fictional "Trudy" forming October 15. It's not real data.

**Base rates (my rough estimates, not from a source)**
- Mid-October is past the Eastern Pacific peak, but hurricanes still happen then. In recent years, as best I recall, very few had a hurricane active between October 15 and 17. 2015, a strong El Niño year, did (Olaf). Most of 2017–2025 didn't: 2017 had only two storms forming after October 1, and 2022's late storm Roslyn came around October 22. I'd put the climatological rate at roughly 20–35%, probably higher in an active El Niño year like this one.

**What to watch before October 15**
- NHC Eastern Pacific outlooks (every 6 hours) and any Sergio advisories: when it forms, its forecast peak, and whether NHC's 5-day forecast reaches October 15 at 64 knots or more.
- Any further development south of Mexico, which is common in El Niño Octobers.
- Rachel's final advisories.

**Prediction markets:** I didn't find any.

**Sources:**
- [1](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/gtwo.php)
- [2](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/tcr/?season=2026&basin=epac)
- [3](https://weather.substack.com/p/october-4-2026-sunday-tropical-update)
- [4](https://cdapress.com/news/2026/oct/05/a-very-active-pacific-hurricane-season/)
- [5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_Pacific_hurricane_season)

criterios: This question resolves YES if, at any point between 00:00 UTC on October 15, 2026 and 23:59 UTC on October 17, 2026, the U.S. National Hurricane Center (NHC) has an active tropical cyclone in the Eastern Pacific basin (east of 140°W) classified as a hurricane — i.e. a system for which NHC issues a public advisory reporting maximum sustained 1-minute surface winds of at least 64 knots (74 mph). This can be confirmed from NHC's Eastern Pacific Tropical Weather Outlook and advisory archive at https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/?epac . A system first reaching hurricane strength before October 15 but still classified as a hurricane during the window counts. If no such advisory is issued during the window, the question resolves NO.
letra_pequena: Only the Eastern Pacific basin (east of 140°W) counts; Central Pacific (140°W–180°) and other basins do not. Post-storm reanalysis is irrelevant — resolution is based on the operational classification reflected in NHC advisories issued during the window. If NHC's website is temporarily unavailable, archived advisories (e.g. via the NHC advisory archive or [credible sources](https://www.metaculus.com/faq/#definitions)) will be used.
razonamientos:
(a) **Time left:** About eight days until the window opens on October 15, and eleven days until the outcome is known after October 17.

(b) **Status quo:** No qualifying hurricane is currently confirmed for that window. Rachel is a hurricane now, but is unlikely to remain one in the Eastern Pacific through October 15.

(c) **Reference class:** Hurricanes active in the Eastern Pacific during a particular three-day mid-October window are uncommon—roughly 20–35% in the research assistant’s estimate. This active El Niño season raises the chance above an ordinary year.

(d) **No scenario:** Rachel weakens or crosses 140°W, while the developing system forms too late, stays below hurricane strength, or weakens before October 15.

(e) **Yes scenario:** A new storm develops soon, reaches hurricane strength, and remains east of 140°W during October 15–17.

(f) **Deciding technicality:** An **NHC operational public advisory issued during the window** must report winds of at least 64 knots for a cyclone east of 140°W. A later reanalysis upgrade would not count.

Probability: 31%

(a) **Time left:** About 8 days until the window opens on October 15, and 11 days until it closes.

(b) **Status quo:** No qualifying hurricane is currently known to be active during October 15–17. Rachel is unlikely to remain a hurricane east of 140°W that long.

(c) **Reference class:** A hurricane active in the Eastern Pacific during a particular three-day window in mid-October is uncommon—roughly a 20–35% event by the research assistant’s estimate. The active El Niño season raises the odds, though the narrow window matters.

(d) **No scenario:** Rachel weakens or crosses 140°W, and the next developing system either fails to reach hurricane strength or does so outside the window.

(e) **Yes scenario:** A system forming south of Mexico in the next several days strengthens to a hurricane and remains east of 140°W during October 15–17.

(f) **Deciding technicality:** An **NHC advisory issued during the window** must report winds of at least 64 knots for a cyclone **east of 140°W**. A later reanalysis finding hurricane strength would not count.

The potential new system makes Yes plausible, but its formation, intensification, and timing must all line up.

Probability: 30%

(a) **Time left:** The window opens October 15, eight days from now, and closes October 17 at 23:59 UTC. The answer will be known about ten days from today.

(b) **Status quo:** No hurricane is forecast for October 15–17. Rachel is moving west over cooler water toward 140°W and should weaken or leave the basin well before October 15. Sergio has not formed yet. If nothing changes, the answer is No.

(c) **Reference class and base rate:** I checked Eastern Pacific seasons from about 2004 to 2025 for a hurricane active between October 15 and 17. My recollection finds only three or four clear cases: Rick in 2009, Paul in 2012, and Olaf in 2015. Several other years came close but missed:
- 2023: Norma reached hurricane strength on October 18.
- 2022: Roslyn formed around October 20.
- 2018: Sergio ended around October 10, and Willa came around October 20.

That gives a climatological rate of roughly 15–20%. Strong El Niño years (2009, 2015) do better, and this hyperactive El Niño season raises the odds.

(d) **No scenario:** Sergio forms around October 7–9. It either stays a tropical storm or peaks as a hurricane around October 11–13, then weakens over cooler water or moves past 140°W before October 15. No other system reaches hurricane strength until after October 17.

(e) **Yes scenario:** Sergio forms around October 8–11, moves slowly south of Mexico, and becomes a hurricane by October 13–15 while still in warm water. Alternatively, another disturbance (common in El Niño Octobers) forms around October 10–12 and is a hurricane by October 16–17.

(f) **Technicalities:**
- The system must be east of 140°W while NHC is advertising it at 64 knots or more.
- A Central Pacific hurricane does not count. Rachel crossing 140°W as a hurricane would not help.
- Operational advisories decide it; post-storm reanalysis does not.
- Any single advisory at 64 knots or more during the 72-hour window is enough.

**Weighing it up:** A named storm is likely forming soon, and it is an active El Niño year. But the timing has to line up within a narrow three-day window, and a storm forming now would most likely peak and fade before October 15. On balance I put it modestly above the base rate.

Probability: 30%
